title: What happens when a ky request fails?
feature: Follow a failing GET request from `ky.get()` through retries and hooks until it rejects, then find where you would change the retry rules.

ref.excerpt: ky[method] = (input: Input, options?: Options) => createRequest(input, () => validateAndMerge(defaults, options, {method}));
ref.note: Every HTTP method shortcut calls createRequest

ref.excerpt:
const defaultRetryOptions: InternalRetryOptions = {
	limit: 2,
	methods: retryMethods,
	statusCodes: retryStatusCodes,
	afterStatusCodes: retryAfterStatusCodes,
	maxRetryAfter: Number.POSITIVE_INFINITY,
	backoffLimit: Number.POSITIVE_INFINITY,
	delay: attemptCount => 0.3 * (2 ** (attemptCount - 1)) * 1000,
	jitter: undefined,

steps.title: Start at the call you write
steps.explanation: You call `ky.get(url)`. Every method shortcut on the default instance is a thin wrapper: it merges your options with the defaults and hands off to `createRequest`, which calls `Ky.create()`.

claims.text: `ky.get`, `ky.post` and the other shortcuts all go through `createRequest`.

refs.excerpt: ky[method] = (input: Input, options?: Options) => createRequest(input, () => validateAndMerge(defaults, options, {method}));

claims.text: If setting up the request throws, you get a rejected promise rather than a synchronous throw.

activity.prompt: To see what actually happens to the request, which file would you open next?

options.label: source/core/Ky.ts
options.feedback: `createRequest` calls `Ky.create()`, and the `Ky` class lives here. This is where the request lifecycle is.

options.label: source/utils/merge.ts
options.feedback: `validateAndMerge` only combines your options with the defaults. It never sends anything.

ref.excerpt: ky[method] = (input: Input, options?: Options) => createRequest(input, () => validateAndMerge(defaults, options, {method}));

options.label: source/types/ky.ts
options.feedback: That file only declares the `KyInstance` type. Types describe the shape, not the behaviour.

steps.title: Ky.create() owns the outcome
steps.explanation: `Ky.create()` builds a `Ky` instance and awaits its private `#run()` method. Whatever `#run()` throws is caught here and passed to `#throwProcessedError()`. Keep that `catch` in mind: it is where a failed request finally leaves ky.

claims.text: Errors from the whole request lifecycle end up in one `catch` block in `Ky.create()`.

activity.prompt: Suppose `#run()` throws an `HTTPError`. What happens before your code sees it?

options.label: Your `beforeError` hooks get a chance to inspect or replace it
options.feedback: Right. `#throwProcessedError()` loops over `hooks.beforeError`, and a hook can return a different error to throw instead.

options.label: Nothing, it is rethrown unchanged
options.feedback: Not quite. The `catch` calls `#throwProcessedError()`, which runs `beforeError` hooks first.

options.label: It is logged and the promise resolves with `undefined`
options.feedback: ky never swallows errors here. `#throwProcessedError()` always ends with `throw`.

steps.title: A 500 arrives
steps.explanation: `#run()` sends the request through `#retry()`, then checks the response. If it is not `ok`, ky builds an `HTTPError`, reads the error body into `error.data`, and hands it to `#retryFromError()`.

claims.text: A non-2xx response becomes an `HTTPError` only when `throwHttpErrors` allows it.

activity.prompt: A GET request gets a 500 back. With default options, what does `#run()` do next?

options.label: Throws the `HTTPError` straight to your code
options.feedback: Not yet. The error is passed to `#retryFromError()` first. It only reaches your code if retrying is refused or exhausted.

options.label: Builds an `HTTPError` and passes it to `#retryFromError()`
options.feedback: Exactly. Building the error and retrying are separate. The error object travels into the retry logic, which decides whether to try again.

options.label: Returns the response so you can check `response.ok`
options.feedback: That only happens when `throwHttpErrors` is turned off.

steps.title: What an HTTPError carries
steps.explanation: An `HTTPError` keeps the `response`, the `request` that actually failed, and the normalised `options`. `#run()` also fills in `data` with the parsed body before any hooks run.

claims.text: The response body is already consumed when you catch the error, so `error.response.json()` will not work.

refs.excerpt: The response body is automatically consumed when populating `error.data`, so `error.response.json()` and other body methods will not work. Use `error.data` instead. The `error.response` object is still available for headers, status, etc.

activity.prompt: You catch an `HTTPError` and want the JSON the server sent back. Where do you read it?

options.label: `error.data`
options.feedback: Yes. `#run()` sets `httpError.data` from the response before throwing.

options.label: `await error.response.json()`
options.feedback: The body has already been read to fill `error.data`, so reading it again fails.

ref.excerpt: The response body is automatically consumed when populating `error.data`, so `error.response.json()` and other body methods will not work. Use `error.data` instead. The `error.response` object is still available for headers, status, etc.

options.label: `JSON.parse(error.message)`
options.feedback: The message is built from the status, method and URL, not the body.

steps.title: Should ky try again?
steps.explanation: `#calculateRetryDelay()` is a series of gates. Any gate can `throw error`, which ends retrying. If every gate passes, it returns how long to wait. The defaults it compares against live in `normalize.ts`.

claims.text: By default ky retries twice, on status codes 408, 413, 429, 500, 502, 503 and 504.
POST is not in the default retry methods, because repeating it could create something twice.

activity.prompt: In `#calculateRetryDelay()`, click the line that stops a failed POST request from being retried.
activity.hint: Look for the gate that checks the request method.

steps.title: Hooks along the way
steps.explanation: ky calls your hooks at fixed points. For a GET that keeps failing, the attempt loop repeats `fetch`, `afterResponse` and `beforeRetry` until the limit is reached. `beforeRequest` only runs once, before the first attempt.

claims.text: `beforeRequest` hooks run once per call and always see `retryCount: 0`.
`beforeRetry` hooks see the attempt number they are about to start.

activity.prompt: Put these in the order they first happen for a GET that fails, is retried, and eventually gives up.
activity.feedback: `init` runs inside `Ky.create()` before the instance exists. `#run()` calls `beforeRequest`, then `#retry()` fetches. `afterResponse` sees the 500, `#retryFromError()` runs `beforeRetry`, and once retries run out the `catch` in `Ky.create()` runs `beforeError`.

steps.title: Make a change
steps.explanation: Imagine the maintainers agree that ky should also retry `425 Too Early` by default. You now know every place involved in that decision.

claims.text: Adding a status code to the default list is enough for GET requests to retry it, because the status gate reads `retry.statusCodes`.

activity.prompt: Where is the smallest correct change?

options.label: Add `425` to `retryStatusCodes` in source/utils/normalize.ts
options.feedback: Yes. It is a one-line change to the defaults, and every gate keeps working as before.

options.label: Add an `if (status === 425)` check in `#calculateRetryDelay()`
options.feedback: It would work, but it bypasses the configurable list, so users could not turn it off with `retry.statusCodes`.

options.label: Change the `HTTPError` constructor
options.feedback: `HTTPError` only describes a failure. It plays no part in deciding whether to retry.

steps.title: Prove it works
steps.explanation: ky's retry tests start a local server that counts requests. To prove your change, you would copy a test that fails with a retryable status and check the request count. Run them with `npm test`.

claims.text: With the default limit, a retried request is sent `defaultRetryCount + 1` times in total.

activity.prompt: Your new test sends 425 twice, then 200. What should it assert?

options.label: The body is returned and the server saw 3 requests
options.feedback: Right. That mirrors the existing "status code 500" test: success on the third attempt proves both retries happened.

options.label: The call throws an `HTTPError` with status 425
options.feedback: That would prove 425 is still not retried, the opposite of your change.

options.label: The server saw exactly 1 request
options.feedback: One request means no retry happened. Compare the "only on defined status codes" test, which asserts exactly that for a 400.
